newsitem.title: GERMANY: German stores hope new hours boost Christmas trade.
newsitem.headline: German stores hope new hours boost Christmas trade.

text.p: Poor weather on Monday evening dampened the first full day of Germany's new era of longer shopping hours, but big retailers said on Tuesday they were still hopeful business would take off as Christmas approaches.
At the start of the month, Germany finally introduced new shop hours to replace outdated regulations from the 1950s that had forced stores to close at 6.30 p.m. during the week.
Shops can now open until eight p.m. on weekdays and two hours later to four p.m. on Saturdays. Monday was the first day of extended across Germany because of a holiday last Friday.
Big retailers reported a mixed picture, with stores in major city centres generally posting a sales pickup and businesses outside main shopping areas less lively.
"Business went normally," Julie Edelmann-Veith, spokeswoman for department store chain Kaufhof, a unit of German retail giant Metro AG, said.
Edelmann-Veith said drizzle in parts of the country had kept shoppers away on Monday, usually a slow day anyway.
Karstadt AG, Kaufhof's main competitor, said its stores in prime locations, like Cologne's city centre, had shown a gain of up to 15 percent compared to the same day last year.
"Business was very steady throughout the day and into the evening," Karstadt spokeswoman Monika Franke said.
Sales at bigger out-of-town shopping centres, seen as likely to take business away from neighbourhood stores, also improved.
Germany's Retail Federation (HDE) noted that city centre stores in Berlin and Munich did well but suburban and small-town shops waited in vain for customers.

Stores in cities like Essen and in suburban locations also did not fare as well, partly due to problems informing consumers of later shopping times and getting city authorities to lay on extra late public transportation.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, who fought union and retailer resistance to extend shop hours, called the change a "breakthrough" that would have an impact on Germany's whole economic landscape.
But, on a tour with journalists on Monday evening through Bonn's city centre stores, Rexrodt found that shop managers did not plan to take on extra staff to cover extra shifts.
"The labour costs are simply too high," furniture store owner Jan Graff told Rexrodt.
So, instead of taking advantage of the longer hours, many stores had closed by seven p.m., prompting TV crews to turn their cameras away from Rexrodt to shuttered storefronts.
But some stayed optimistic with holidays approaching.
"With the Christmas period, the longer hours should start to have an impact," Edelmann-Veith said.

Though stores were reluctant to predict big sales gains in the runup to Christmas, retail analysts expected a boost for bigger stores. WestLB said in a research note that Karstadt would increase sales by four percent in the fourth quarter.
HDE said a straw poll of stores showed consumers needed to get used to the longer hours.

"The big Christmas rush is still to come," HDE spokesman Thomas Werz said. "No retailer should allow himself to be unsettled by the odd situation at the beginning of this week and should stay open late at least until the end of the year."
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
